docs.title: Chrono Batch Render
docs.text:
Chrono Batch Render is a physically-based, real-time, spectral renderer for planetary robotics and sensing, with C++ and Python APIs.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text:
Chrono Batch Render is built on these open-source projects.

  • Vulkan Headers, volk and Vulkan Memory Allocator for the GPU layer
  • Slang for shaders
  • DLPack for sharing tensors with PyTorch, JAX, Warp and NumPy
  • nanobind for the Python bindings
  • OpenEXR and Imath, stb, Basis Universal and bc7enc_rdo for images and textures
  • NanoVDB for volumes
  • nlohmann/json for JSON
  • {fmt} for text formatting
  • tinyobjloader for OBJ import
  • MikkTSpace for tangents
  • NVTX for profiling
  • OpenUSD for scene interchange
  • Dear ImGui and GLFW for the viewer
  • GoogleTest for tests
  • Google Benchmark for benchmarks

Chrono Batch Render also leverages ideas from these renderers and projects:

  • Madrona for batch rendering across many worlds
  • Chrono::Sensor for sensor simulation inside Chrono
  • Cycles, Mitsuba 3 and PBRT for physically based and spectral rendering
  • OpenUSD and Omniverse Fabric for the schema-based scene
  • ovrtx for zero-copy interops and USD-based rendering
  • nvpro-samples for Vulkan ray tracing and cluster LOD
  • PANGU for planetary and asteroid surface simulation
  • IRIS for real-time, closed-loop rendering of space sensors
  • CosmoScout VR for planet-scale scenes and solar-system visualization
  • three-geospatial for atmospheres and clouds
  • Isaac Lab and Newton for tiled cameras in robot learning

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Chrono Batch Render ships as a Python package on PyPI, as C++ packages on GitHub releases, as a Docker image, and builds from source everywhere else.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Supported Linux x86_64 and aarch64 (glibc 2.34) Windows x64 and ARM64 macOS 26 or later on Apple silicon Python 3.10 or later

Chrono Batch Render renders on any device it has a backend for.

Backend Devices Driver Vulkan NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs, Apple GPUs through MoltenVK, and CPUs through lavapipe Vulkan 1.3 or later CUDA NVIDIA GPUs CUDA 12.0 or later HIP AMD GPUs, both CDNA and RDNA ROCm 6.2 or later Metal Apple GPUs In progress CPU x86_64 and aarch64 CPUs through Embree In progress

Ray tracing hardware is optional. On devices without it, Chrono Batch Render builds and traverses its own BVH in software, so every backend renders the same scenes. Hardware texture sampling is optional too, and devices without it filter textures in software.

On macOS, the Vulkan backend runs on Apple GPUs through MoltenVK, which Homebrew installs along with the Vulkan loader. macOS doesn't search Homebrew's library folder, so point DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH at it too, and add that line to your shell profile to keep it.

brew install molten-vk vulkan-loader
export DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH=$(brew --prefix)/lib

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
pip install chrono-batch-render

Wheels are built for Linux, Windows and macOS. Check the install by listing the devices Chrono Batch Render can render with.

chrono-batch-render --devices
python -c "import chrono_batch_render; print(chrono_batch_render.__version__)"

docs.title: Viewer
docs.text:
The chrono-batch-render wheel includes the interactive viewer. It needs a GPU that can present to a window.

chrono-batch-render

With no options, the chrono-batch-render command opens the viewer on the default scene, and chrono-batch-render --help lists its options. From Python, open a viewer on your own scene.

import chrono_batch_render
import chrono_batch_render.viewer

device = chrono_batch_render.Device(backend=chrono_batch_render.Backend.VULKAN, presentation=True)
scene = chrono_batch_render.Scene(device)
viewer = chrono_batch_render.viewer.Viewer(scene, product="/Render/View")
viewer.run()

docs.title: Without a window
docs.text:
The chrono-batch-render command also renders the default scene without a window, which needs no display. --output writes the last frame's AOVs to a folder, --worlds clones the scene into several worlds with one image each, and --preset picks real-time or minimal shading.

chrono-batch-render --output frames --size 640x360 --aovs DistanceToCamera,Normal --worlds 4

--benchmark times steps one at a time and three in flight, after --warmup steps, and --json prints the timings as one line for scripts. --profile adds the profiler's report of where the time went.

chrono-batch-render --benchmark --frames 200 --size 1280x720 --json
chrono-batch-render --headless --frames 60 --profile

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
Download the archive for your platform from the latest release. It holds the library, its C++17 headers, the CMake package and a pkg-config file. The Linux archives are built against glibc 2.34, so they run on any distribution from the requirements.

Releases follow tags, so latest points at the newest one. The commands below install the latest release from the command line. On Linux and macOS, look up its version first.

VERSION=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render/releases/latest \
    | sed -nE 's/.*"tag_name": *"v([^"]+)".*/\1/p')

Set VERSION yourself to install another release.

LinuxmacOSWindows 
URL=https://github.com/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render/releases/download/v$VERSION
curl -fL $URL/chrono-batch-render-$VERSION-Linux-$(uname -m).tar.gz \
    | tar -xz -C ~/.local --strip-components=1

URL=https://github.com/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render/releases/download/v$VERSION
mkdir -p ~/.local
curl -fL $URL/chrono-batch-render-$VERSION-macOS-aarch64.tar.gz \
    | tar -xz -C ~/.local --strip-components=1

$Release = Invoke-RestMethod https://api.github.com/repos/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render/releases/latest
$VERSION = $Release.tag_name.TrimStart("v")
$URL = "https://github.com/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render/releases/download/v$VERSION"
$ARCH = if ($env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE -eq "ARM64") { "aarch64" } else { "x86_64" }
Invoke-WebRequest "$URL/chrono-batch-render-$VERSION-Windows-$ARCH.zip" -OutFile chrono_batch_render.zip
Expand-Archive chrono_batch_render.zip .
Rename-Item "chrono-batch-render-$VERSION-Windows-$ARCH" chrono-batch-render

Each release also lists a SHA256SUMS file to check the downloads against.

The Windows ZIP holds both Debug and Release builds, so either configuration links against it. Add the chrono-batch-render folder to CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH so CMake finds it, and its bin folder to PATH so programs built against it find the DLLs.

Then find it from CMake and link against chrono_batch_render::chrono_batch_render.

find_package(chrono_batch_render REQUIRED CONFIG)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE chrono_batch_render::chrono_batch_render)

Chrono Batch Render's headers need only C++17, so projects on C++17 or later can use the packages. chrono_batch_render::chrono_batch_render asks CMake for C++17 at least, and with pkg-config pass -std=c++17 or later yourself. Building Chrono Batch Render itself needs C++20.

docs.title: Viewer
docs.text:
The archives also hold the viewer library and the chrono-batch-render command line tool. The viewer is a separate library, so projects that only link chrono_batch_render::chrono_batch_render don't load it or the windowing libraries it opens. To use it, ask CMake for the viewer component and link against chrono_batch_render::viewer.

find_package(chrono_batch_render REQUIRED CONFIG COMPONENTS viewer)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE chrono_batch_render::viewer)

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The image is Ubuntu 24.04 with Chrono Batch Render installed in /opt/chrono-batch-render.

docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render

Tags follow releases, so 0.1.0, 0.1 and latest, where latest is always the newest final release. Release candidates such as 0.1.1rc1 only get their own tag. Add --gpus all to render on an NVIDIA GPU, which needs the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host.

CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH already points at Chrono Batch Render, so a project mounted into the container can build against it.

docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/app" -w /app ghcr.io/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render \
    sh -c "cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja && cmake --build build"

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
Chrono Batch Render needs CMake 3.25 or later and a C++20 compiler, such as GCC 12, Clang 18 or Visual Studio 2022. Its other dependencies are downloaded while it configures.

git clone https://github.com/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render.git
cd chrono-batch-render
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_INSTALL=ON
cmake --build build
cmake --install build --prefix ~/.local
Option Default Builds CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_BUILD_PYTHON OFF The Python bindings CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_BUILD_VIEWER OFF The viewer that the chrono-batch-render command opens, which needs X11 and Wayland development files on Linux CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_BUILD_TESTS OFF The C++ and Python tests CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS OFF The benchmarks CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_INSTALL OFF The install rules and packages CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_COVERAGE OFF Code coverage instrumentation, with GCC or Clang

The Python package builds from the checkout with pip. It includes the viewer, so on Linux it needs the X11 and Wayland development files, which these packages provide on Ubuntu.

sudo apt-get install libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev
pip install .

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
The presets build the way CI does, each in its own folder.

Preset Builds ci Release with the tests, in build-ci bench Release with the benchmarks, in build-bench coverage Debug with coverage and the tests, in build-coverage package The TGZ archive on Linux and macOS, viewer included, in build-package package-windows The Windows ZIP with Debug and Release builds, in build-package-windows 
cmake --preset ci
cmake --build --preset ci
ctest --preset ci

The tests run on the device Chrono Batch Render picks by default, which CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_ADAPTER and CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_BACKEND change. To run them on others, list the adapter aliases that chrono-batch-render prints in CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_TEST_ADAPTERS, separated by commas, or set it to all.

CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_TEST_ADAPTERS=vulkan:0,cuda:0 ctest --preset ci

CI sets CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_TEST_FULL=1 to run the full suite. It tests every device and also compiles every kernel for every NVIDIA and AMD target, which the tests otherwise skip.

cmake --preset package
cmake --build --preset package
cpack --preset package

docs.title: Kernel cache
docs.text: Chrono Batch Render compiles its kernels the first time they run and keeps them in a cache, so later runs start quickly. The cache lives in ~/.cache/chrono-batch-render on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/chrono-batch-render on macOS and %LOCALAPPDATA%\chrono-batch-render\cache on Windows, and CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_CACHE_DIR moves it anywhere else. Kernels sit in kernels, keyed by their sources and compiler, so versions share the ones that didn't change, and the cache stays under 1 GiB by dropping the least recently used. Deleting the folder is always safe.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If chrono-batch-render --devices lists nothing, no backend found a driver to load. Install your GPU vendor's driver, or lavapipe for the CPU as in Requirements.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: An overview on how Chrono Batch Render is versioned, branched, tagged and published.

docs.title: The Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Cut release-X.Y from main and bump main to the next minor.
  2. RC by tagging vX.Y.0rc1 on the release branch.
  3. Fix on main, cherry-pick onto the release branch and tag the next RC.
  4. Release by dropping the RC suffix and tagging vX.Y.0.
  5. Patch with the same loop on the same branch, tagging vX.Y.1, vX.Y.2 and so on.

Pushing a v* tag runs release.yml, which publishes the following.

Output RC tag vX.Y.ZrcN Final tag vX.Y.Z PyPI prerelease (needs pip install --pre) release GitHub release marked prerelease release with assets and SHA256SUMS Docker (GHCR) X.Y.ZrcN X.Y.Z, X.Y, plus latest if newest Docs not deployed X.Y/, plus latest if newest

docs.title: Where the version lives
docs.text:
File RC tag Final tag CMakeLists.txt project(... VERSION X.Y.Z) set set CMakeLists.txt CHRONO_BATCH_RENDER_PRERELEASE "rcN" "" CITATION.cff version, date-released unchanged update README.md BibTeX version unchanged update CHANGELOG.md unchanged move [Unreleased] to [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD
  • CMakeLists.txt is the source of truth. The Python package version is read from it.
  • CI fails any tag that doesn't match VERSION + PRERELEASE.
  • On main, VERSION is always the next minor with an empty PRERELEASE.

docs.title: Cut a release branch
docs.text:
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c release-X.Y
# CMakeLists.txt: VERSION X.Y.0, PRERELEASE "rc1"
git commit -am "Set version to X.Y.0rc1"
git push -u origin release-X.Y

Then commit straight to main to set VERSION to the next minor.

docs.title: Tag an RC
docs.text:
• [ ] Fixes are on main and cherry-picked with git cherry-pick -x
  • [ ] PRERELEASE bumped to rcN
  • [ ] CI is green on release-X.Y
  • [ ] git tag -a vX.Y.ZrcN -m "Chrono Batch Render X.Y.ZrcN" && git push origin vX.Y.ZrcN
  • [ ] Release workflow is green
  • [ ] Smoke test with pip install --pre chrono-batch-render==X.Y.ZrcN and docker pull ghcr.io/uwsbel/chrono-batch-render:X.Y.ZrcN

docs.title: Tag a final release
docs.text:
• [ ] Last RC tested with no changes since, apart from version metadata
  • [ ] PRERELEASE "" in CMakeLists.txt
  • [ ] CITATION.cff, the README.md BibTeX and CHANGELOG.md updated
  • [ ] CI is green on release-X.Y
  • [ ] git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "Chrono Batch Render X.Y.Z" && git push origin vX.Y.Z
  • [ ] Release workflow is green (PyPI, GitHub release, Docker, docs)
  • [ ] Smoke test with pip install chrono-batch-render==X.Y.Z
  • [ ] CHANGELOG, CITATION and README edits ported back to main

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Tag only on release-X.Y branches, never on main. The release workflow fails any vX.Y.Z tag whose commit is not on release-X.Y.
  • Fix on main first and cherry-pick with -x. Commit straight to the release branch only for release-only fixes.
  • Release branches take fixes only, never features.
  • Use annotated tags (git tag -a).
  • Never move or reuse a tag that reached PyPI. Ship the next version instead.
  • RC numbers are cheap. When in doubt, cut another RC.
  • A final tag should match the last RC apart from the version metadata.
  • Keep a release branch open for as long as that minor series is supported.

docs.title: Branch model
docs.text: main is always the next minor version. Each minor series gets a long-lived release-X.Y branch that only takes fixes, and every release (RC or final) is a tag on that branch.

docs.title: 1. Cut the release branch
docs.text:
Branch release-0.1 from main, tag the first RC, and bump main to 0.2.0.

gitGraph
    commit id: "feature work"
    commit id: "ready for 0.1"
    branch release-0.1
    checkout release-0.1
    commit id: "set 0.1.0rc1" tag: "v0.1.0rc1"
    checkout main
    commit id: "bump to 0.2.0"

docs.title: 2. Fix a bug found in the RC
docs.text:
Fix on main, cherry-pick, bump the RC and tag again. Repeat until an RC is clean.

gitGraph
    commit id: "ready for 0.1"
    branch release-0.1
    checkout release-0.1
    commit id: "set 0.1.0rc1" tag: "v0.1.0rc1"
    checkout main
    commit id: "fix A"
    checkout release-0.1
    cherry-pick id: "fix A"
    commit id: "set 0.1.0rc2" tag: "v0.1.0rc2"

docs.title: 3. Ship the final release
docs.text:
Drop the RC suffix, update the changelog and citation, tag, and port those edits back to main.

gitGraph
    commit id: "ready for 0.1"
    branch release-0.1
    checkout release-0.1
    commit id: "set 0.1.0rc2" tag: "v0.1.0rc2"
    commit id: "release 0.1.0" tag: "v0.1.0"
    checkout main
    commit id: "port 0.1.0 changelog"

docs.title: 4. Patch an existing release
docs.text:
Same loop on the same branch. Nontrivial fixes get an RC (v0.1.1rc1) first.

gitGraph
    commit id: "ready for 0.1"
    branch release-0.1
    checkout release-0.1
    commit id: "release 0.1.0" tag: "v0.1.0"
    checkout main
    commit id: "fix B"
    checkout release-0.1
    cherry-pick id: "fix B"
    commit id: "release 0.1.1" tag: "v0.1.1"
    checkout main
    commit id: "port 0.1.1 changelog"

docs.title: 5. Start the next minor series
docs.text:
Cut release-0.2 the same way. release-0.1 stays open, and a fix that affects both is cherry-picked onto each.

gitGraph
    commit id: "ready for 0.1"
    branch release-0.1
    checkout release-0.1
    commit id: "release 0.1.0" tag: "v0.1.0"
    checkout main
    commit id: "0.2 features"
    branch release-0.2
    checkout release-0.2
    commit id: "set 0.2.0rc1" tag: "v0.2.0rc1"
    checkout main
    commit id: "bump to 0.3.0"
    commit id: "fix C"
    checkout release-0.1
    cherry-pick id: "fix C"
    commit id: "release 0.1.2" tag: "v0.1.2"
    checkout release-0.2
    cherry-pick id: "fix C"
    commit id: "set 0.2.0rc2" tag: "v0.2.0rc2"

docs.title: When something goes wrong after tagging
docs.text:
• Failed before PyPI published, so delete the tag, fix and retag the same version.
  • Failed after PyPI published, so re-run the failed jobs and keep the tag.
  • Broken RC, so fix and tag the next RC.
  • Broken final release, so fix and ship the next patch, and yank on PyPI if it's harmful.

Deleting a tag.

git tag -d vX.Y.Z && git push origin :refs/tags/vX.Y.Z
gh release delete vX.Y.Z --yes

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Each minor series gets its own copy of the docs, with a version picker in the header. CI builds them with mike and commits the built site to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. The deploy lives in .github/workflows/docs-deploy.yml.

  • gh-pages holds one folder per version (dev, 0.1, 0.2) plus latest and a root redirect.
  • Only CI writes to gh-pages. Don't edit it or merge it by hand.
  • Doc fixes go on main like any other change, and get cherry-picked onto a release branch if that version's docs need them.
  • A release branch's docs only redeploy with its next final tag.
When Docs go to Push to main /dev/ (with coverage) Final release 0.1.1 /0.1/ RC not deployed
  • The site root and /latest/ always show the newest final release.
  • Patching an older series never takes over /latest/.
  • Before the first release, /latest/ shows dev.
  • Docker's latest tag works the same way.
